issue_text: The combined age of Peter, Paul and Jean is 100 years old. Find the age of Peter knowing that Paul is 18 years older than John and that Peter’s age is equal to the sum of Paul and John's age.
summary: The task is a three-way age word problem: the ages of Peter, Paul and John sum to 100, Paul is 18 years older than John, and Peter's age equals Paul's plus John's. The run is a four-turn AG2 MathChat dialogue between mathproxyagent and the assistant, and it converges with no retry, no error and no revision. T1 is the proxy's framing turn: it fixes the tooling (Python, sympy, fractions over decimals), enumerates three candidate solution routes, decomposes the hardest route into steps, and pre-specifies a replan branch for an invalid result. T2 carries almost all of the cognitive load: the assistant selects the system-of-equations route, translates each clause of the problem into one equation, names sympy as the solver, and emits a complete script that builds three Eq objects, calls solve, and prints the answer. T3 is the proxy relaying one line of execution output, Peter's age is 50 years old, and T4 accepts it and boxes 50. The answer is correct (J=16, Q=34, P=50), but the verification is thin: nothing in T4 substitutes 50 back into the three constraints, so "The solution has been verified" rests on the script having run without raising rather than on any check. The problem statement's own inconsistency, naming Jean in the first sentence and John in the other two, is silently normalized at T2 and never surfaced.

findings.title: The framing turn out-plans the solving turn
findings.body: Under action-level quoting, T1 alone fires five spans of planning-side work - tool choice, an output-format requirement, a three-option strategy menu, step decomposition, and a conditional replan rule - before the assistant has said anything. T2, the turn that actually solves the problem, opens with a single strategy span and then moves straight to formalization and code.

findings.title: Verification is asserted rather than performed
findings.body: T4's only evaluative span, The solution has been verified, follows a turn whose entire content is one line of stdout. No span in the run re-substitutes 50 into P+Q+J=100, Q=J+18 or P=Q+J, so the Goal-completion check is grounded in the absence of a traceback, not in a constraint check.

findings.title: "Jean" is normalized to "John" without comment
findings.body: The problem names Jean in its first sentence and John in the other two. T2's variable-definition span maps the cast to P, Q, J with John in Jean's place, and no span anywhere in the four turns flags the mismatch or asks the proxy about it.

findings.title: The executable weight sits in Grounding, not Executing
findings.body: Quoting the dialogue surface puts the sympy solve call under Grounding (tool invocation) and T3's stdout relay under Grounding (peer messaging). The only Executing span in the whole run is T4's boxed final answer, which is a fair picture of a dialogue where the solver never runs anything itself.

turns.headline: Agent models the three ages as equations and writes sympy code.
turns.action:
This problem can be approached by creating a system of equations. Let's denote Peter's age as P, Paul's as Q, and John's as J. According to the problem, we have the following equations:

1. P + Q + J = 100 (The combined age of Peter, Paul, and John is 100 years old)
2. Q = J + 18  (Paul is 18 years older than John)
3. P = Q + J (Peter’s age is equal to the sum of Paul and John's age)

Using sympy, we will be able to solve this system of equations.

Here is the Python code to solve this:
```python
from sympy import symbols, Eq, solve

# define the symbols
P, Q, J = symbols('P Q J')

# define the equations
eq1 = Eq(P + Q + J, 100)
eq2 = Eq(Q, J + 18)
eq3 = Eq(P, Q + J)

# solve the system of equations
solution = solve((eq1,eq2,eq3), (P, Q, J))

# print the solution
print(f"Peter's age is {solution[P]} years old.")
```
The output will be the age of Peter.
